splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether they can be selected afterward. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be determined as of the statutory measurement date (end of prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of the most current data available.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the judgment's specified time when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during periods of absconding, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to judicially create such a doctrine.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars re-raising claims previously presented — when filing successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter bar than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing a categorical prohibition in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that (b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions; prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to ballot-counting rules. The split affects whether voting procedure disputes must wait until post-election, potentially affecting rules on mail-in voting and ballot counting deadlines nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when state laws affect the counting of ballots in ways they allege are unlawful.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge state election laws pre-election because their alleged injury is too speculative or generalized.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) in interpreting ambiguous Sentencing Guidelines provisions that affect criminal liability or punishment.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity or agency deference should prevail when interpreting ambiguous Sentencing Guidelines. At least three circuits hold that lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit panel held that deference trumps lenity. This split has deepened after Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability without proper lawmaking.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary controls over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines enhancements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to be met for disqualification) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether 'and' in the safety-valve provision means defendants must meet all three listed criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This directly affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference when the guideline text itself does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and attempt in the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid interpretation deserving deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses. This affects whether many defendants qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 reasonably interprets ambiguous guideline text and is entitled to controlling weight, so conspiracy counts as a 'controlled substance offense' for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text — no deference
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond what the text allows, so conspiracy is not a 'controlled substance offense.'

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), may be considered as an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law — particularly the elimination of mandatory stacked § 924(c) sentences — as a factor supporting compassionate release. Some circuits categorically bar such consideration, while others allow it. SCOTUS has granted cert to address the issue.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, including the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment, as one factor among others in the extraordinary-and-compelling analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, whether alone or in combination with other factors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for the underlying violation of supervised release at revocation, or whether revocation sentences may only account for the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a sentence upon revocation of supervised release may be imposed to punish the defendant for the conduct that violated the conditions, or whether it may only reflect the breach of the judicial trust. The Sixth Circuit's Lewis precedent allows express punishment, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split.

positions.label: Revocation sentence may punish for underlying conduct
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly consider and punish the defendant for the underlying violation conduct when imposing a revocation sentence for supervised release.

positions.label: Revocation sentence may only address breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that sentences upon revocation of supervised release should reflect the breach of the court's trust, not punish for the new criminal conduct that violated the conditions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule covers a substance not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the 'controlled substance offense' definition in USSG § 4B1.2(b) requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be federally controlled. Some circuits hold that any state-law drug offense qualifies, while others require a federal-schedule match. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: State-law offense qualifies regardless of federal schedule
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' broadly includes offenses under state law without requiring the substance to be federally controlled.

positions.label: Substance must also be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction only qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' if the substance at issue is also on the federal schedules, applying a categorical approach that requires a federal-schedule match.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal of a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order in a criminal case is governed by the civil appeal deadline (60 days when the government is a party) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the longer civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal proceeding (requiring a 14-day notice of appeal). The Seventh Circuit joined what it described as the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline (60 days when the government is a party) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion remains part of the criminal proceeding, requiring the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the duration of custody (such as First Step Act time-credit determinations) must proceed via habeas corpus or may use civil rights actions like Bivens.
splits.description: A longstanding and unresolved circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions or incidents of confinement that may affect duration of custody must be brought exclusively through habeas corpus or may also be pursued through civil rights actions. This affects prisoners challenging BOP decisions on First Step Act earned time credits.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-related claims
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges the fact or duration of confinement, including BOP decisions on credit calculations affecting release, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy.

positions.label: Habeas and civil rights claims may coexist
positions.summary: Holds that conditions-of-confinement claims are cognizable under both habeas and civil rights statutes, and that habeas is not necessarily the exclusive remedy for all claims touching on duration of confinement.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Carmona v. U.S. Bureau of Prisons

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and a good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This matters significantly for debtors whose home values increase during their Chapter 13 case.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A), read in light of § 541(a)'s broad definition of 'property of the estate,' means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtors
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) limits the converted estate to the value of property as of the original petition date, meaning post-petition appreciation belongs to debtors who convert in good faith.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable as a collateral order because medical privacy is a value of 'high order,' joining the First Circuit's approach. Other circuits have not extended the collateral order doctrine to sealing orders generally, creating a potential circuit disagreement.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal medical records are effectively unreviewable on appeal from final judgment and protect a 'high order' privacy interest warranting immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal is not a collateral order because the interest can be adequately vindicated through other means, such as post-judgment appeal or protective orders.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release can serve as a vehicle for addressing claims that overlap with habeas relief under § 2255. Some circuits allow consideration of legal errors or unfairness as one factor in compassionate release, while others hold that such claims must be brought exclusively through § 2255 proceedings.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors in compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider claims related to potential errors in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for § 2255-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release cannot be used to address claims that are properly the domain of § 2255 habeas proceedings, and such claims cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
